title: Associative containers and data-structure choice
lead: Distinguish ordering, unique keys, average hash cost and access side effects.
why: A catalogue needs ID lookup, a log needs word frequencies, and a report needs reproducible order. One container rarely fits every operation. Choose from the contract rather than always reaching for vector or unordered_map.
objectives: Choose set, map or unordered_map by contract.
prerequisites: Modules 1–3: validated input, functions, vector, records, references and lifetimes.
Direct learning dependencies: cpp.search-linear-binary, cpp.structures. New constructs are explained before the task.

sections.title: Keys, mapped values and uniqueness
paragraphs: A set stores keys; a map associates each key with a mapped value. In a frequency index, the word is the key and its occurrence count is the value. Repetition updates the count rather than adding a distinct key. Record-ID uniqueness is a separate domain rule: equal amounts may be allowed while duplicate IDs are not.

A map element resembles a pair: first is the key and second the mapped value. const auto& entry reads without copying; const auto& [word,count] names the parts through a structured binding. Do not mutate a map key in place because it would break lookup organization. Changing a key needs an explicit erase/insert design or another documented operation.

sections.title: Ordered map and set
paragraphs: std::map and std::set keep keys under their comparator’s order. Lookup, insertion and erasure have logarithmic guarantees under their contracts. Balanced trees are common implementations, but the public interface does not require knowing a particular balancing scheme. Ordered traversal is useful when the report actually needs it.

Ordered-container uniqueness uses comparator equivalence: neither a precedes b nor b precedes a. This need not equal an arbitrary user-defined operator==. Our integers and ASCII strings use compatible ordinary ordering. Do not make lookup case-insensitive while insertion follows another order.

sections.title: Unordered containers: hash and equality
paragraphs: unordered_map and unordered_set use hashing to organize lookup and equality to distinguish keys. Different keys can share a hash: a collision does not permit dropping one record. Many operations have constant-like average cost in element count under appropriate conditions; their worst case can be linear.

Equivalent keys must have equal hashes, and the chosen rules must stay consistent. Hashing and comparing strings inspect content, so O(1) in key count does not mean independence from string length. The lab bounds ASCII keys to twelve bytes, keeping input and comparison assumptions explicit.

sections.title: A read must not silently insert
paragraphs: counts[word] inserts a missing key with a default-initialized mapped value. For int that is zero, making ++counts[word] useful for counting. But counts["missing"]==0 mutates the container even though it looks like a read. Use find and compare with end when asking whether a key exists, preserving map size.

end must not be dereferenced here either. Check the result before reading second. at can report absence with an exception; this runtime is not the EH teaching environment, so the lab uses explicit find. Distinguish a missing key from an existing mapped zero, which can represent a different domain state.

sections.title: Invalidation is container-specific
paragraphs: Do not transfer vector rules to unordered_map without checking its contract. Rehash reorganizes buckets and invalidates iterators, while references and pointers to surviving elements remain valid under that operation’s rules. Erasure invalidates access to the erased item. reserve can rehash, so an earlier iterator is not automatically safe afterward.

Before iterating while inserting, determine whether rehash can occur; collecting changes separately is often simpler. A user catalogue can keep stable IDs and repeat find instead of storing iterators long-term. Valid iterators alone do not prevent logically stale data: an index must match the current dataset version.

sections.title: Collisions and a testing scaffold
paragraphs: The supplied SameHash returns zero for every int, forcing collisions while equality still distinguishes keys. operator()(int) const makes its object callable so the container can obtain a hash value. Reading this scaffold is sufficient here; designing generic hash libraries belongs to a later module.

Check insertion, lookup of every key and erasure of one key. The experiment demonstrates collision correctness; it neither measures production performance nor makes the intentionally poor hash appropriate. A container hash is not a cryptographic primitive or a promise against adversarial input.

sections.title: Deterministic reports and catalogue reconciliation
paragraphs: Do not expect stable unordered traversal across libraries, runs or rehashing. For a report, copy pairs into a vector and sort by key, or use an ordered map. Storage, lookup and presentation can use different structures; that is an explicit architectural boundary, not merely duplication for prettier stdout.

The cumulative practicum compares catalogues over a union of keys. For each ID distinguish old-only, new-only and both; compare values in the last case. find does not manufacture the absent side. Validate both inputs before reporting, or a malformed second catalogue can falsely resemble mass deletion.

sections.title: Choose by workload and check independently
paragraphs: List insertions, point queries, range queries and ordered reports in the workload. A small immutable dataset can favor a sorted vector over a tree or hash; frequent mutation changes the tradeoff. Include preparation, memory, key length and worst-case guarantees rather than relying on an O(1) slogan.

Test emptiness, repeated keys, different insertion orders, invalid words and duplicate IDs. Compare frequencies with an independent scan of the original list. Save an explicitly ordered report. Next, a reproducible data generator will show why a seed alone does not make a whole experiment portable.

blockPracticum.title: Practicum: reconcile two catalogues
blockPracticum.challenge: Read n m, then n id value pairs for an old catalogue and m pairs for a new one. Each has 0…32 records; id=1…9999 is unique within its catalogue and value=−10000…10000. In id order print removed id old, new id value, or changed id old new; omit unchanged records. Print no-change if nothing differs. Reject errors and extra tokens as invalid.
walkthrough: Separate validation of both inputs, key union, comparison and report construction. A valid first catalogue does not justify a partial report when the second is malformed.
find does not create a missing record. Every union key has three essential cases: old only, new only, or both. Unchanged data is a subcase of the last case.
